title: How to Forget Someone: 12 Ways to Let Go and Heal
h1: How to Forget Someone: 12 Healthy Ways to Let Go and Start Healing
description: Learn how to forget someone you loved with 12 practical, healthy steps: create distance, process your feelings, rebuild routines and move forward.
excerpt: Twelve practical, compassionate steps to stop dwelling on someone you loved, from creating distance to rebuilding a life that feels like yours again.
intro:
You can’t delete a person from your memory, and honestly, you wouldn’t want to. They were part of your story. What you can do is reach a point where thinking of them no longer stops you in your tracks, where their name is just a name and your days belong to you again.

That’s what learning how to forget someone really means: loosening the grip, not erasing the past. Whether it was an ex, a situationship or someone you never quite dated, the steps below will help you create distance, work through the hurt and build a life that feels full without them in it. Healing isn’t linear, but it is very possible.
body:
Why it’s so hard to stop thinking about someone

When you’re attached to someone, your brain builds habits around them: the good-morning text, the weekend plans, the person you tell first when something happens. When the relationship ends, those habits keep firing. You reach for your phone, you scroll back through photos, you imagine conversations. That isn’t weakness. It’s how attachment works.

The goal, then, is to gently retrain those habits and give your heart time to catch up with your head. Here’s how.

12 ways to forget someone and move forward

1. Stop revisiting the memories on purpose

Rereading old messages and replaying favorite moments keeps the wound fresh. You’ll still think of them, especially at first, but try not to go looking for those memories. When you catch yourself reaching for the old thread, put the phone down and do something else for ten minutes.

2. Put their things out of sight

The hoodie, the concert ticket, the mug they always used. You don’t have to throw everything away in a dramatic purge. A box in a closet, or returning items through a friend, works just as well. Out of sight really does help it become out of mind.

3. Clean up your digital space

Archive photos into a hidden folder, mute or unfollow their accounts, and remove their number from your favorites. You can decide later whether to keep or delete things for good. Right now, you’re reducing surprise reminders that set you back.

Tip: Muting is a great middle ground. It removes them from your feed without the emotional weight of unfriending, and you can revisit the decision when you feel stronger.

4. Keep your mind and calendar busy

Empty evenings are when thoughts spiral. Fill some of that time with things that absorb your attention: a class, a workout, a new show, cooking a complicated recipe, volunteering, or seeing friends. You’re not avoiding your feelings forever, just giving your mind other places to go.

5. Talk it out with people you trust

Saying things out loud to a friend or family member takes away some of their power. You don’t need advice every time; sometimes you just need to be heard. Choose people who support your healing rather than people who stir up drama.

6. Rebuild your confidence

Endings can leave you questioning your worth. Make a list of things you like about yourself, revisit goals you set aside, and do things you’re good at. Our guide on how to be happy with yourself is a good place to start.

7. Stop checking their social media

Checking on them, even “just to see,” keeps you emotionally tied. Every glimpse restarts the cycle of wondering and comparing. If you’re tempted, ask a friend to hold you accountable, or use app timers to break the habit.

8. Accept what happened, at your own pace

Acceptance doesn’t mean you’re fine with how things ended. It means you stop fighting the reality that they did. Let yourself feel sad, angry, relieved or all three. Feelings that are allowed tend to pass more quickly than feelings that are pushed down.

9. Forgive, for your own sake

Forgiveness isn’t saying what they did was okay, and it doesn’t require reconciliation. It’s choosing to set down resentment so it stops taking up space in your life. Some people find it helpful to write a letter they never send, saying everything they wish they could.

10. Take care of your body and mind

Sleep, food, movement and time outside all affect your mood more than we like to admit. Go for walks, cook real meals, drink water and get some sunlight. Gentle routines give your emotions a steadier base to heal from.

11. Go no contact (or as close as you can)

Every “just checking in” text reopens the door. Give yourself a clean break for a meaningful stretch of time. If you share kids, work or a friend group, keep contact brief, polite and focused on logistics. For more on this, see how to stop thinking about your ex.

12. Focus on the present moment

Much of the pain lives in the past (“we used to”) or the future (“we were going to”). Bringing yourself back to now, through mindfulness, journaling or simply noticing what’s around you, reduces the pull of both.

A simple daily routine for letting go

If the advice above feels like a lot, try this small daily structure for the first few weeks:

  • Morning: Write three lines about how you feel and one thing you’re looking forward to.
  • Midday: Get outside for at least ten minutes.
  • Evening: Do one thing just for you, whether it’s a hobby, a call with a friend or a long shower.
  • Before bed: Leave your phone across the room so late-night scrolling doesn’t pull you back in.

What to do when the memories come back

They will, often at random moments: a song in a store, a restaurant you used to visit, the anniversary of your first date. When it happens:

  • Name it. “Okay, I’m thinking about them again.”
  • Let it pass. Notice the feeling without following it down a rabbit hole.
  • Redirect. Text a friend, take a walk or turn to a task.

Over time, these moments get shorter and less intense. That’s progress, even if it doesn’t feel like it.

How long does it take to forget someone?

There’s no exact timeline. It depends on how long you were together, how deep the connection was, how it ended and what support you have. Some people feel much better in a few weeks; for others it takes many months. Comparing your pace to anyone else’s only adds pressure.

A more useful measure: are the good days slowly outnumbering the hard ones? If so, you’re healing. For more on this stage, read how to get over a broken heart.

Things that slow healing down

  • Rebounding quickly to avoid feeling the loss.
  • Staying “friends” before you’re genuinely ready.
  • Keeping tabs on them through mutual friends.
  • Blaming yourself for everything, or nothing.
  • Numbing out with alcohol or endless distraction.
Tip: If weeks turn into months and you still struggle to get through daily life, or you feel hopeless, consider talking with a licensed therapist. Getting help is a sign of self-respect, not failure.

Building a life you love again

The best way to forget someone isn’t to focus on forgetting at all. It’s to build a life so full that they gradually take up less room. Reconnect with friends you drifted from, pursue goals you postponed, try things you’ve always been curious about. Our list of things to do to move on from a breakup has plenty of ideas, and how to move on after a breakup covers the bigger picture.

The bottom line

Learning how to forget someone is really learning how to let go. Create some distance, allow yourself to feel it, care for your body and mind, and slowly fill your days with things that are yours. One day you’ll realize you haven’t thought about them in a while, and that it doesn’t hurt when you do.
takeaways: You won’t erase someone completely, but you can loosen their hold on your days.
Reduce reminders: put things away, mute accounts and stop checking their profiles.
Let yourself feel the loss; suppressed feelings tend to linger longer.
No contact, healthy routines and support from friends speed up healing.
Build a full life of your own so they gradually take up less space.

faq.q: How do I forget someone I love deeply?
faq.a: Start by creating distance: limit contact, put reminders away and stop checking their social media. Then let yourself grieve, lean on friends and keep your days structured with things you enjoy. Deep love takes time to soften, so be patient with yourself and measure progress in good days, not perfect ones.

faq.q: Is it possible to completely forget someone?
faq.a: Usually not, and that is okay. Memories of important people tend to stay. What changes is how they feel. With time and healing, thinking of them becomes neutral or even fond rather than painful, and they stop shaping your choices and moods.

faq.q: Should I delete pictures of my ex?
faq.a: You do not have to decide right away. Moving photos to a hidden folder or archiving them removes daily reminders without a permanent choice. Later, when emotions are calmer, you can decide whether to keep a few, store them away or delete them.

faq.q: Why can’t I stop thinking about someone?
faq.a: Your brain built habits and hopes around them, and those take time to fade. Unresolved feelings, ongoing contact, checking their profiles and having lots of unstructured time can all keep thoughts looping. Reducing contact and filling your time with meaningful activities helps the habit weaken.
